organizations.csv: organization.organization_id is required, but c01 is null in 13 rows (1.3%) and its 1017 parsed values cover only 999 distinct numbers, so roughly 18 rows repeat an account number. Blank and duplicate keys must be resolved before load because contact, subscription and activity rows reference this id and identical ids with different content are a 409 conflict.

Customer rule 2 (no recorded activity in 18 months -> force Inactive) cannot be applied from this file: there is no activity or last-contact column unless the answer to the c14 question says otherwise. Sequence the organization load after the activity extract, or re-run the status rule once activity data is available.

Rules 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 are all subscription-level and have no effect on this dataset. Rule 4 (Strategic accounts always carry an Enterprise plan) will need the 85 Strategic accounts from c09 to be reconciled against the subscriptions file at that stage.

c08 and c14 both contain dates after today (4 and 5 rows respectively, up to 2027-09-03). A future organization.customer_since is implausible and these rows should be reviewed at validation; the field has no constraint that would reject them.

c12 shows 39 malformed addresses and 30 duplicates after normalization. contact.email is only required to be unique within an organization, so cross-organization duplicates are acceptable, but duplicates sharing the same c01 would collide with the one-primary-contact rule; handle at validation.

c02 has 49 values with stray whitespace and 11 case-variant groups, which may indicate the same company recorded more than once under slightly different spellings. Worth a dedupe pass against c01 before load.

I assumed c12 and c13 describe the same single person (the account's primary contact) and therefore generate one contact record per organization, per rule 1. If the CRM contacts extract also contains these people, reconcile on lowercased email to avoid creating a second contact for the same person.
contacts.csv: All column names in this file are opaque codes (c01, c16-c23), so every mapping here is inferred from type, shape, cardinality and the customer's business rules rather than from names. A data dictionary or a 10-row sample reviewed by the customer would materially raise confidence, particularly for the two boolean columns and the date.

Volume check against rule 1: 1046 distinct account keys in c01 and roughly 942 true values in c21 suggests about 100 accounts have no flagged primary contact. Per rule 1, those should be resolved from `primary_contact_email` on the account row during the accounts load; coordinate the two loads so that at most one contact per organization ends with is_primary = true.
22 rows (1.0%) have no value in c01, yet contact.organization_id is required and must reference an existing organization. Those rows cannot load as-is; disposition is a validation-step decision.

Email quality: 106 values are malformed and there are 66 normalized duplicates across 33 case-variant groups. Since email is required and must be unique within an organization, expect rejects or merges once c01 and c18 are normalized; handle at validation.
Phone quality: no value is currently in E.164 and 88 will not normalize to a valid number after stripping formatting.

c22 contains 8 future-dated values (up to 2027-08-05) and only 16.6% of values are ISO-formatted across six distinct date formats, including the ambiguous %m/%d/%y - parsing order must be fixed deterministically before any use of this column.

Ordering dependency: organizations must be loaded before these contacts (target cross-record rule 1), and the c01 -> organization_id string formatting must match exactly what the accounts load writes into organization.organization_id.
subscriptions.json: Rule 11 (trial subscriptions older than 90 days are dead and must not be migrated) needs a cut-off date to be implementable: the 84 rows with status 'trialing' and the 27 rows with plan 'Trial' must be filtered against a reference date agreed with the customer (go-live date or export date). The engineer should apply this filter before load rather than mapping those rows.

Rule 7 (Legacy Gold -> enterprise unless seats < 10) depends on c28, which is null in 4.1% of rows (41 records). Where a Legacy Gold row has no seat count, the plan cannot be derived deterministically; decide a fallback at validation.

subscription.seats is required but c28 has 41 nulls, and subscription.status/plan/billing_cycle are required with full population, so seats is the only required field with gaps. Default handling for those blanks is a validation-step decision.

Rule 4 says Strategic accounts always carry an Enterprise subscription and that billing is wrong where it disagrees. This cannot be checked inside this dataset; after joining c01 to the accounts export, any Strategic account whose plan resolves to starter or professional should be overridden to enterprise. Flag the count to the customer before applying it.

c01 is only 90% unique (903 distinct over 1003 rows), i.e. roughly 100 organizations hold more than one subscription. Every c01 value must resolve to an organization loaded first (cross-record rule 1); unmatched values will reject.

Cross-record rule: an inactive or churned organization cannot hold a trial or active subscription. Rule 2 (dormant accounts become Inactive) and rule 6 (Closed accounts are churned) will push some organizations to inactive/churned while their subscription here still resolves to active or trial. Reconcile the two loads before go-live.

Dropping c32 loses the currency marker on 75 CAD rows. If finance needs to find them after go-live, consider recording the original currency on the related organization via organization.tags, or keeping the source file for the true-up.
c29 has 2 future dates and c30 has 80; the 80 on c30 are expected for renewals, the 2 on c29 (future start dates) are worth a sanity check at validation.
activity.csv: This dataset is the evidence base for customer business rule 2 (accounts with no activity in the last 18 months are dormant and must be loaded as organization.lifecycle_status = 'inactive'). The engineer should derive, per c01, the latest c35 value and feed it back into the organization load; it cannot be expressed as a field mapping here.

c35 ranges to 2026-09-11, i.e. future-dated events relative to a present-day migration. If the dormancy calculation in rule 2 uses max(occurred_at), future rows will keep accounts out of dormancy. Flag the future-dated rows to the customer at validation.

Only 1000 distinct values appear in c01 while the activity table has 4947 rows; every one of those 1000 account numbers must already exist as an organization.organization_id before the activity load, per the cross-record rules. Any c01 value with no matching organization will reject.

Coverage of c32 (USD on 2563 rows) and c36 (1913 parseable amounts, 650 placeholders, 3034 nulls) does not line up: roughly 650 rows carry a currency code with a placeholder instead of an amount. That is a validation-time cleanup, but worth confirming no amounts are being silently dropped.
c34 has one case-variant group (Invoice / INVOICE, 1489 rows combined); the mapping table normalizes this, no data loss expected.
c35 has 4946 distinct values over 4947 rows, so exactly two activities share a timestamp. Harmless given activity_id is unique.
Assumption: c36 amounts are already in the activity currency and need no conversion, consistent with rule 12 which says amounts migrate as-is into USD and finance trues up after go-live.

rows.reason: Integer 5-digit values with 98.2% uniqueness on the organization row read as the legacy account number, and the catalog says 'the customer's legacy account number usually lands here'. It is also the join key that contact/subscription/activity rows will reference.
Free text, no nulls, 996 distinct values with company-like shapes ('Aaaaaa AAA', 'Aaaaa-Aaaaa') on an organization dataset; organization.name is the only required string label in the entity.

The value set (Active/Inactive/Prospect/Churned/On Hold/Closed) is account lifecycle vocabulary and maps onto the required enum prospect|active|inactive|churned; customer rule 6 explicitly tells us how to read the two non-enum values.

Short sector codes (MFG, CONST, LOG, TECH, HC, ENR, PS, OTH) line up one-to-one with the organization.industry enum; the 45 rows holding numeric codes ('31', '23') look like NAICS sector prefixes and need confirmation.

Mixed two-letter codes ('AB', 'GA') and full names ('Colorado') with 55 distinct values is a US state / Canadian province column, which is exactly organization.billing_region (state or province code). It is also the column rule 5 tells us to use to disambiguate country 'CA'.

Country names and codes (US, USA, United States, U.S., Canada, CAN, CA, MX, Mexico) map to the required ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 organization.billing_country. The 42 'CA' rows are the case customer rule 5 warns about (Canada vs California).
URL-shaped values (scheme://www.domain.tld) on an organization row; organization.website is the only url field in the catalog.

A date column on the organization row, and organization.customer_since is the only organization-level date in the catalog. However the file carries two near-identical date columns (c08 and c14) and nothing in the names says which is the relationship start, so the assignment needs confirmation.

Gold/Silver/Bronze/Platinum/Strategic is the customer_tier of rule 3; 'Strategic' maps cleanly to organization.account_priority = strategic, but the catalog warns account_priority is operational treatment and only offers standard|priority, so how the spend bands collapse into those two is a business decision.

Currency-formatted amounts from $100,000 to $45,000,000 with a mean around $23M on an organization row are company revenue, matching organization.annual_revenue_usd; the magnitudes are far too large for subscription MRR.

Whole numbers from 22 to 3999 on an organization row read as headcount, and organization.employee_count is the natural home. The competing reading is subscription seat count, which matters because rule 7 keys the Legacy Gold plan decision off a <10 seat threshold - though no value here is below 22.

An always-populated, 97% unique email on the account row is the primary_contact_email that customer rule 1 declares authoritative for creating or flagging the primary contact; the organization entity has no email field, so it must land on contact.email.

Two-token person-name shapes ('Aaaaa Aaaaaa', max length 22) alongside the primary contact email; organizations have no name-of-person field, so this belongs on the same derived primary contact and must be split across contact.first_name and contact.last_name.

A second date column with essentially the same range and format mix as c08. Only one organization-level date exists (customer_since), already proposed for c08; a renewal date would belong to subscription.renewal_date, which cannot be written from this file because subscription_id, plan, cycle, status, seats and MRR are not present here.

Four repeated free-text remarks ('acquired by parent co', 'moved HQ 2024', 'renewal call scheduled', 'do not contact billing before 9am') on 55% of rows. They could be labels for organization.tags or genuine notes belonging on activity records (activity.kind = 'note'); that is a business decision about how operations wants to see them.

Fully populated, 100% unique identifier with a consistent 'CT-999999' shape, which reads as the CRM's contact key; it satisfies the contact_id pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$ as-is and gives idempotent writes.

Integer in the 10000-79936 band with only 1046 distinct values across 2279 rows (~2.2 contacts per value), which is the signature of a foreign key to the account; the organization catalog notes that the customer's legacy account number is what lands in organization.organization_id.

Near-unique text with two-token 'Firstname Lastname' shapes and a 27-character max: this is the contact's full name, and the target only offers separate first_name and last_name, so this one column feeds both.
Typed as email with a local@domain shape and 98.6% distinct values; contact.email is the only email field in the target and is required for every contact.
Phone-typed column with North American display formats ((999) 999-9999, 999-999-9999, 999.999.9999); contact.phone is the only phone target and accepts E.164 only.

Twelve free-text job/role labels (Billing, Primary, Technical, CTO, AP, ...) matching the free-text contact roles described in customer rule 13; contact.role is the only enum target for this. The destination is clear but several values need a business decision before the enum mapping is safe.

A boolean in mixed vocabularies whose true values (Y 459 + yes 199 + TRUE 165 + 1 119 = 942) are close to the 1046 distinct organization keys in c01, which fits rule 1's 'exactly one primary contact per account' far better than a marketing opt-out would. The other boolean, c23, is only ~9.4% true and matches rule 14's opt_out, but the column names are opaque codes so the assignment should be confirmed.

A date spanning 2016-2027, but the contact entity in the target catalog has no date field at all (contact_id, organization_id, email, first_name, last_name, phone, role, is_primary). The only plausible home is organization.customer_since on another entity, and that would only be right if this date is the account relationship start rather than a contact-level created/last-contacted date.

A clean Y/N flag that is true in only 214 of 2279 rows, matching the `opt_out = Y` marketing preference described in rule 14; the target catalog has no consent or marketing-preference field on contact, so the flag itself has no home. Rule 14 only requires that opted-out contacts still be migrated, which this mapping honours - the records load, the flag does not.

Fully populated, 100% unique identifier with shape AAA-99999 and 'SUB-' prefix examples; it is the natural primary key of the subscription entity and already satisfies the id pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$.

A 5-digit integer in the 10000-89979 band, fully populated but only 90% unique (903 distinct over 1003 rows), which is the profile of a legacy account number repeated across multiple subscriptions; the catalog notes the legacy account number lands in organization.organization_id, so this is the foreign key to it.

Ten plan-name values (Enterprise, Pro, Professional, Starter, Enterprise v2, Basic, Legacy Gold, Professional Plus, ENT, Trial) that business rules 7 and 8 explicitly translate into the subscription.plan enum; the only value the rules do not cover is 'Trial'.
Six values that are all billing frequencies (M, A, monthly, annual, yearly, Q) and map onto the two-value subscription.billing_cycle enum, with rule 9 telling us what to do with the quarterly ones.

Nine lifecycle values (active/Active, trialing, past due/past_due, canceled/cancelled, paused, expired) that correspond directly to the subscription.status enum, with rule 10 covering the two values that have no direct equivalent.
Eight discrete small integers (5, 10, 15, 25, 40, 60, 100, 250) stored as a mix of int (709) and str (253) - the classic seat-count ladder, and the only integer quantity field on subscription.

One of two unnamed high-cardinality date columns; c29 has the earlier range (2016-12-09 to 2027-08-01) and only 2 future values, which fits a start date, while c30 runs later with 80 future values and fits a renewal date. The assignment rests on distribution, not on the column name, so it should be confirmed.

The later of the two unnamed date columns (to 2027-09-14) with 80 future values, which is what you expect from a forward-looking renewal date; paired with c29 as start_date, subject to the confirmation question.

A money column (0 to 40000, mean 6070.70) stored mostly as text with currency decoration ('USD 60', '$40,000.00', '5100'); subscription.mrr_usd is the only monetary field on the subscription entity and rule 12 states the billing export amounts are already monthly.

Currency code (USD 928, CAD 75) with no currency field anywhere in the target catalog; rule 12 makes it redundant because CAD amounts are migrated as-is into the USD-denominated mrr_usd field and finance trues up after go-live. No decision is needed to complete the migration.
Fully populated, 100% unique identifier with an ACT-####### shape that is clearly the activity's own key; it satisfies the activity_id pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$ as-is.

Integer in a tight 10000-10999 band with 1000 distinct values repeating across 4947 rows: this is the legacy account number acting as the parent key, and activity.organization_id is the only reference field on the activity entity.

Eight categorical values (Invoice, Payment, Login, Ticket, Note, Support Ticket, INVOICE, Call) that line up with the activity.kind enum apart from casing variants, two spellings of ticket, and 'Call' which has no enum member.
The only datetime column, fully populated and near-unique per row, which is exactly what activity.occurred_at expects as the event timestamp.

Numeric monetary column present on roughly the same subset of rows as the USD currency code, and activity.amount_usd is the only money field on the activity entity; values 25-10000 are plausible invoice/payment amounts.

A single-valued currency code (USD on all 2563 populated rows) with no currency field anywhere in the target catalog; activity.amount_usd is USD by definition and business rule 12 says amounts migrate as USD regardless, so the column carries no information that survives the migration.

Short free-text-style labels ('escalated: parts delay', 'renewal discussion', 'monthly invoice') that read as the human-readable summary of the event; activity.description is the only text field on the activity entity and it is nullable, which fits the 24.5% blanks.
